Deplore

/dih-PLOR/ - rhymes with door · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Deplore means to express strong disapproval of or sorrow about something.

Her toast began by deploring the whole tradition of toasts, then ran eleven affectionate minutes anyway.

Worked Example

The rulebook's foreword, written by the league's retiring president, spends its two pages deploring what the shot clock has done to the patient possession game he refereed for thirty years: possessions he once counted in minutes now end in seconds, and the crowd, he writes, has learned to cheer the countdown instead of the play. Then the foreword ends, and the shot-clock rules follow it in full.

Deplore is the exact word for those two pages, because it means to express strong disapproval of or sorrow about something — grief and judgment in one breath. Complaining is smaller and wants a fix; deploring mourns aloud and on purpose, whether or not anything can still be done.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

bemoan: groan over — the everyday, slightly weary cousin

lament: pure sorrow with no judgment attached; deplore adds the disapproval

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

applaud: greet with approval

welcome: be glad it came

Where it sits · how loudly the disapproval is voiced — regret → deplore → castigate

regret vs. deplore: Regret is private — a sigh over what happened, said to no one in particular.

castigate vs. deplore: Castigate goes further than deplore — deploring grieves over conduct from a distance; castigating hauls the guilty up by name and flays them for it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-

Prefix — de-: thoroughly

Root — -plore

Root — -plore: to wail, cry out (Latin plorare)

Put it together

Put it together: De- (thoroughly) + plore (to wail) = to weep over completely. Latin deplorare was full-throated mourning; English cooled it into disapproval with the grief still humming inside. The same crying root kneels in implore — to beg tearfully — which is why both words sound like they are down on one knee.

Use the root in a new word: implore

Use the root in a new word: implore: Implore points the wailing at someone: she implored the guards to let the child through.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / elevated

Deplore is disapproval in mourning dress — editorials, resolutions, and grandmothers use it about conduct and losses alike. Lament grieves without judging; bemoan grumbles. And this unit's denigrate and deride attack people, which deplore never quite does — it faults the deed while sorrowing over it.
